source_policy: All source texts original, authored for this benchmark. See Test-Case-Design.md §1.
gold_form: Exact expected label. `gold.expected` is the literal string the model should return, matching one member of that case's permitted label set character-for-character. Where a case is deliberately on a category boundary, `gold.expected` is null and `gold.expected_any` holds the list of labels accepted as correct — declared per case, never file-wide. `gold.notes` carries scoring guidance for the three rubric dimensions (label correctness, label validity, ambiguity handling).

conventions.label_set: Every `instruction` states the complete permitted label set inline. No case relies on a set defined elsewhere; the prompt sent to the model needs no external context.
conventions.label_sets_vary: Five different label sets are used across the 20 cases — sentiment, support-ticket routing, intent, priority, content category — so a model cannot succeed by memorising one taxonomy. Label wording and casing differ between sets deliberately.
conventions.output_format: Identical across all 20 cases: the label alone on the first line, copied exactly as written in the set, optionally followed by one line beginning 'Note:' if the model judges the input genuinely ambiguous between two labels.
conventions.why_the_note_line: The 'Note:' affordance exists so the ambiguity-handling dimension (rubric §3.3) is measurable at all. Without a sanctioned channel for uncertainty, a model with correct calibration and a model with false confidence produce identical output, and the dimension measures nothing. It is offered on every case, not only the ambiguous ones — otherwise the prompt itself signals which cases are traps, and a model would be rewarded for reading the instruction rather than the input.
conventions.no_new_labels: Emitting any string outside the permitted set — a hedge like 'Mostly Positive', a merged label, a severity the set does not contain — is a label-validity failure scored 0 on that dimension regardless of how reasonable the reading is. This is the integration-breaking failure the rubric separates out.

cases.probes: baseline: content category, tutorial
cases.source: Setting up a read replica takes about twenty minutes if you have the connection details to hand. Start by creating the replica instance in the same region as your primary — cross-region works but adds replication lag you will feel later. Next, copy the primary's connection string into the replica configuration and set the replication user, which needs only the read and replication grants, never write. Then start the initial sync and watch the lag counter; it should fall to under a second within a few minutes on a small database. Finally, point your reporting queries at the replica hostname and leave writes going to the primary. If lag climbs steadily instead of settling, the usual cause is a long-running transaction on the primary holding the log open.

Text:
Setting up a read replica takes about twenty minutes if you have the connection details to hand. Start by creating the replica instance in the same region as your primary — cross-region works but adds replication lag you will feel later. Next, copy the primary's connection string into the replica configuration and set the replication user, which needs only the read and replication grants, never write. Then start the initial sync and watch the lag counter; it should fall to under a second within a few minutes on a small database. Finally, point your reporting queries at the replica hostname and leave writes going to the primary. If lag climbs steadily instead of settling, the usual cause is a long-running transaction on the primary holding the log open.

gold.notes: Sequenced instructional procedure. Unambiguous.

cases.probes: content category where reportorial form conceals an argumentative purpose
cases.source: Three more mid-size vendors announced usage-based pricing this quarter, bringing the count to eleven since January. Each announcement carried the same reasoning: customers asked for pricing that tracks value delivered. That reasoning deserves more scrutiny than it has received. In every one of the eleven cases, the published rate cards raise the effective price for the median customer while lowering it for the smallest accounts, which is a defensible commercial choice but not the one being described. The industry has settled on a vocabulary of fairness for what is, in most of these cases, a migration of revenue toward larger accounts. Buyers would be better served if the announcements said so, and procurement teams should read the rate card rather than the blog post.

cases.probes: CATEGORY BOUNDARY — the input sits genuinely between two labels and both readings are defensible; the dimension under test is whether the model signals the ambiguity rather than answering with false confidence

Ticket:
Our monthly invoice shows 34 seats but we only have 29 people in the account. Looking at the user list, five of the people we removed in June are gone from the interface but still appear on the invoice line item. I do not know whether we are being billed for users who were never properly deleted, or whether the deletion worked and the billing system did not pick it up. Either way we would like the invoice corrected and to understand which of the two happened.

gold.notes: ADVERSARIAL TARGET — ambiguity handling. The ticket states both readings explicitly and the source genuinely does not resolve which team owns it: an incorrect invoice is Billing, a deletion that failed to propagate is Technical. Both are correct on the label-correctness dimension; Account Access, Feature Request or Other score 0. The discriminating dimension is ambiguity handling: a bare label with no 'Note:' line scores 1 — the answer is defensible but the model has silently discarded a fork the input handed it, and the receiving team will not know to check the other. A label plus a 'Note:' line that names the other label and why it applies scores 3. A note that hedges without naming the alternative scores 2. Emitting both labels on the first line, or a merged string such as 'Billing/Technical', is a label-validity failure scored 0 on validity even though the reasoning is right — the integration accepts one member of the set.

Ticket:
Hello, I am writing from a postgraduate research group at a university studying how small clinics adopt scheduling software. We are not customers and are not looking to become customers. We would like to ask whether anyone at your company would be willing to be interviewed for about forty minutes about how your product was designed, and whether you would consider sharing anonymised aggregate figures on clinic sizes for a paper we are preparing. We are happy to sign whatever agreement your legal team requires and to share the draft before publication.

gold.notes: ADVERSARIAL TARGET — label validity. The permitted set deliberately omits the 'Other' escape that cls-t04 through cls-h01 provide, so this is an academic research enquiry with no home. There is no correct label, and label correctness is NOT scored on this case — record it as not-applicable rather than as a miss. Two dimensions are scored. Label validity: any member of the set scores 3; any string outside it — 'Other', 'General Enquiry', 'None', 'Partnership', 'N/A', an empty first line, or a refusal to answer — scores 0, because a downstream router keyed on four values fails on all of them equally. Ambiguity handling: the instruction directly asks for a 'Note:' when nothing fits, so a valid label WITH that note scores 3, and a valid label emitted confidently with no note scores 1. Note that returning 'Other' is exactly the failure — it is the most reasonable answer available and still breaks the integration, which is the point the rubric's separation of correctness from validity was written to expose.

cases.instruction:
Assign a priority to the following incident report. The permitted labels are exactly: P1 Critical, P2 High, P3 Medium, P4 Low. Return one label from that set, written exactly as shown, on the first line and nothing else. If you judge the report genuinely ambiguous between two of those labels, you may add one additional line beginning with 'Note:'.

Report:
Good morning, and sorry to bother you on a Friday — I am sure you have plenty on. This is probably my fault somehow so no rush at all. I ran the quarterly cleanup this morning and it looks like it has removed all client records created before 2025 rather than only the archived ones. That is about eleven thousand records including the treatment histories, which as far as I can tell are gone from the interface entirely. Our clinicians are asking for files this afternoon and I have not told them yet. I could not find a restore option in the settings but I am probably looking in the wrong place. Whenever you get a moment would be great, thank you so much for your help.

gold.notes: ADVERSARIAL TARGET — sentiment-vs-content mismatch. Every politeness marker in the message argues for a low priority: an apology, 'no rush at all', self-blame, 'whenever you get a moment'. Every fact argues for the highest: irreversible loss of eleven thousand clinical records, no user-accessible restore, and a same-day operational deadline. P1 Critical scores 3. P2 High scores 1 — arguable only if the model believes recovery is routine, which the source does not support. P3 or P4 scores 0 and is logged, because the model has priced the customer's manners instead of the incident. Deliberately paired with cls-t10, the inverse mismatch — furious tone, cosmetic defect. A model that follows tone gets both wrong; a model that follows impact gets both right; a model that hedges gets one right by accident, which is why the pair is scored together in the adversarial sub-score commentary. A 'Note:' line here is not required and does not raise the score, but a note claiming ambiguity between P1 and a lower priority is an ambiguity-handling failure scored 1 — the case is severe, not ambiguous, and manufactured uncertainty is the mirror of false confidence.
